plan.healthButtonTitle: Organisation problems AI-written code tends to pile up: loops, dead code, copies, shortcuts
plan.healthNone: Nothing to point out: no loops, dead files, copies or shortcuts were found.
plan.healthIntro: Information only: nothing here blocks anything. The limits are set in codetac.structure.json ("smells").
plan.healthBecauseFolder: it is in a folder that frameworks often load by themselves
plan.healthBecauseName: its name is often an entry point
plan.healthBecausePublic: it is served as it is from a public folder and may be loaded by its address
plan.healthBecauseVendor: it was copied from a component library (shadcn/ui, see components.json), where parts you do not use yet are normal
plan.healthBecauseByName: another file names its module in a text, to load it by name, which the reading cannot follow
plan.smell_cycle_why: A change in one can break the other, and an AI editing one of them rarely sees the loop. It also makes them hard to move or test apart.
plan.smell_skipped_layer: {from} runs in the browser and uses {to} directly, although the project has its own server routes.
plan.smell_skipped_layer_why: Browser code that talks straight to the database or to an outside service shows its keys and logic to anyone. Going through the server routes keeps them private.
plan.smell_coupling_uses_all_why: A change anywhere can affect it: a sign that it mixes too many jobs.
plan.smell_coupling_used_by_all_why: A change there can break the whole project, so changes to it need extra care.
plan.smell_file_uses_many_why: It does too much: splitting it makes changes smaller and safer.
plan.smell_duplicate_why: A fix made in one copy is easily missed in the others. AI assistants copy code often; one shared function is easier to keep right.
plan.smell_dead_file: {file} is not imported by any file, and no framework or script starts it.
plan.smell_dead_file_possible: {file} is not imported by any file, but it may still run: {because}
plan.smell_dead_file_why: Dead code misleads you and the AI: it gets read, copied and fixed although it never runs.
plan.smell_large_file_why: Large files are hard to review, and an AI editing them tends to rewrite or cut parts it was not asked to touch.
plan.smell_unused_export: {name} in {file} is exported, but no file of the project imports it.
plan.smell_unused_export_possible: {name} in {file} is exported and no file imports it, but it may be kept on purpose: {because}
plan.smell_unused_export_why: It is probably left over from an earlier version; removing it makes the file easier to follow.

public-secret: A variable with a secret's name has the framework's public prefix.
The build puts its value in the code sent to every browser, so anyone can read it.
secret-in-browser: A variable with a secret's name is read in code that runs in the browser.
There its value is empty; adding the public prefix to fix it would expose the secret.
env-tracked: Its values are in the repository's history, and in every copy of it.
env-not-ignored: The next 'git add' would put its values in the repository.
env-no-git: .env files in a folder without git.
Nothing says which files must stay private when the project is shared.
literal-key: A key is written in the code.
Anyone who sees the code can use it; keys belong in variables set outside the code.
no-rls-browser: A table with row level security off is read or written directly from the browser.
With the public key, anyone can read or change every row of it.
used-not-defined: The code uses a table that no schema file defines.
The table may be missing, misspelled, or created by hand outside the project.
defined-never-used: A schema file defines a table that no code uses.
It may be left over, or used by something outside the project.
cycle: Files import each other in a loop.
A change in one can break the other, and an AI editing one rarely sees the loop.
skipped-layer: Browser code uses the data or outside-service layer directly although the project has its own server routes.
Its keys and logic are shown to anyone; going through the server keeps them private.
coupling: A block or file is linked to too many others.
A change there reaches many places, or it mixes too many jobs.
duplicate: The same code is copied in several places.
A fix made in one copy is easily missed in the others.
dead-file: A file that no file imports and nothing starts.
Dead code misleads people and AI assistants: it gets read, copied and fixed although it never runs.
large-file: It is hard to review, and an AI editing it tends to rewrite parts it was not asked to touch.
unused-export: Something exported that no file of the project imports.
It may be dead code, or used from outside the project.
kinds.change: A difference between two versions of the project's structure, found by comparing them.

system.block:
You explain one block of a web project to someone who does not read code easily, for a map of the project.
You get only facts about the block, read from its structure; you never see its code.
In at most 120 words of plain English, say what the block is for and how it connects to the rest.
Use only the facts given. Do not add files, functions, routes, tables, services or effects that are not in them.
Write every name of a file, folder, function, route or block exactly as in the facts, between backticks (`like/this.js`).
If the facts do not say something, do not guess it. Answer only with JSON.
system.plan:
You explain the floor plan of a web project to someone who does not read code easily.
You get only facts about the project, read from its structure; you never see its code.
In at most five short lines of plain English, say what the project is made of, how the parts connect, and what deserves attention.
Use only the facts given. Do not add files, functions, routes, tables, services or effects that are not in them.
Write every name of a file, folder, function, route, table, service or block exactly as in the facts, between backticks (`like/this.js`).
If the facts do not say something, do not guess it. Answer only with JSON.

Use only the facts given. Do not add files, functions, routes, tables, services or effects that are not in them.
Write every name of a file, folder, function, route, table, variable, service or block exactly as in the facts, between backticks (`like/this.js`).
If the facts do not say something, do not guess it. Answer only with JSON.

suggest.system:
You classify the files of a web project into blocks, for a map of the project.
For each file you get only its path and the signatures of what it exports; you never see its code.
Choose the block the path and exports point to. If they do not tell, answer "unknown": never guess.
Give a short reason (at most 15 words) based only on the path and the exports.
Blocks:

blocks.interface: what the user sees and touches: pages, components, styles, browser code
blocks.routes: entry points of the server: HTTP routes, API handlers, server setup, server actions
blocks.logic: the rules of the application: services, calculations, workflows
blocks.data: access to databases: clients, queries, schemas, migrations
blocks.external: calls to outside services: AI, payments, email, other APIs
blocks.config: configuration of the project or the app
blocks.utilities: small generic helpers used everywhere, types

system.purpose:
You write purpose sentences, in English, for people who do not read code easily.
You receive the code of a function and the facts observed when it ran.
Say what the step is for, in one short sentence (at most 15 words), without programming jargon.
Mandatory rules:
- Do not claim effects (writing or reading data, emails, payments, files, calls to external services or to AI) that are not in the observed facts, even if the code could do them.
- Do not mention tables, services, domains or names that do not appear in the facts or in the code.
- Do not invent the business reason: if the code does not show it, describe only what the step does.
- Describe only what happened in this run. Do not describe other branches of the code ("if not…", "otherwise…").
- Do not repeat numbers from the facts; they are already shown beside the sentence.
Answer only with JSON in the requested format. For each boundary listed, give a short sentence explaining what it is for in this step.
system.action:
Summarise in one sentence (at most 25 words), in English, what a user action in an app does, for people who do not read code.
Use only the facts given: the element pressed, the requests, the purposes of the steps and the observed effects.
Do not claim effects that are not in the observed effects. Do not invent the business reason. Answer only with JSON.
system.question:
You answer, in English, a question about one step of an app, asked by someone who does not read code easily.
Use only the facts given: the code of the step, what was observed when it ran and, if present, the recorded values and the lines run.
If the facts are not enough to answer, set "known": false and say in "answer" what is missing, without guessing.
Do not claim effects (writing data, emails, payments, files, external services) that are not in the observed facts.
Tell apart what happened in this run from what the code would do in other cases; if you talk about other cases, say so explicitly.
Answer in at most 120 words, without jargon. Answer only with JSON.

request.system:
A user gave a coding assistant the prompt below. Write what the prompt ASKS FOR, as changes to the structure of the project:
- files: the files to add, change or remove;
- dependsOn: blocks that would start depending on another block;
- services: new external services.
Only what the prompt asks, in its words or as their clear, direct consequence; never what the assistant might also do on its own.
Use the paths from the list for files that exist. A new file only when the prompt names it or clearly needs one, with the path the prompt gives (or the one the project's folders make obvious).
Use only the blocks listed, by their id, and only the services listed, by their name.
If the prompt asks for nothing that changes the structure (a text, a fix inside a function), return empty lists.
note: one sentence, at most 25 words, saying what the prompt asks.

run.help:
Usage:
  codetac [folder] [options] [-- command]   starts the app in the folder (default: the current one) with CodeTAC: Node or Python (FastAPI, Flask)
  codetac diagnose [folder]                  explains what is and what is not working
  codetac report [folder]                    saves the diagnosis to a file to attach to an issue
  codetac structure [folder]                 what the project is made of: its files by block
  codetac structure [folder] --reclassify <file> <block|auto>
                                             places a file in a block yourself (saved in codetac.structure.json)
  codetac structure [folder] --suggest       asks the AI about the Unknown files (shows what is sent first)
  codetac structure [folder] --snapshot [label]
                                             saves the structure as it is now, to compare with later (kept outside the project);
                                             with --predict, first asks what you expect the next change to do, and --diff
                                             then says what you got right
  codetac structure [folder] --snapshots     lists the saved snapshots
  codetac structure [folder] --diff [from] [to]
                                             what changed in the structure: since the newest snapshot, or between two
                                             points (a snapshot id, a commit such as HEAD~3 or a tag, or now)
  codetac hooks [install|uninstall] [folder]
                                             the Claude Code hooks that record each prompt and the files before and after it
                                             (asks first; written in .claude/settings.local.json, nothing else in the project)
  codetac diff [n] [folder] [--code|--open]  what prompt n (the newest by default) changed: files, structure, risks; --code: the lines;
                                             --open: the report in the panel (map, code side by side), with no app running
  codetac diff --list [folder]               the prompts recorded by the hooks
  codetac privacy [--no-ai|--ai] [--on|--off|--default <kind>] [--log [n]] [--clear-log]
                                             what CodeTAC may send to an AI model, a switch for each kind, and the log of what was sent
  codetac help                               this help
  codetac --version                          installed version

Options:
  --script <name>      package.json script to use (default: dev, start…)
  --part <folder>      in a project with several parts, which one to start (can repeat)
  --port <n>           the app's port, if it is not found automatically
  --panel-port <n>     the panel's port (default 4000)
  --minimal            do not follow the project's functions (requests and boundaries only)
  --yes                answer "yes" to the questions (install dependencies, create the .venv…)
  --no-open            do not open the browser
  -- <command>         the start command, when it is not found (e.g. -- node server.js)

hooks.willCreate: CodeTAC will create {file} with three Claude Code hooks:
hooks.willChange: CodeTAC will add three Claude Code hooks to {file}:

keepsOthers.one: Your {count} hook already there stays as it is.
keepsOthers.other: Your {count} hooks already there stay as they are.

hooks.npx: CodeTAC is running from npx's temporary folder, which may be cleaned: install it with npm install -g codetac and run this again.
hooks.what: They archive the project's files (outside the project) when a prompt starts and when it ends, so codetac diff can show what each prompt changed. They print nothing and never block a prompt.
hooks.needsYes: Run it in a terminal to answer, or add --yes.
hooks.notIgnored: git does not ignore {file}; it holds folders of this computer: add it to .gitignore.
hooks.next: From the next prompt in Claude Code (opened in this folder), each prompt is recorded. See them with: codetac diff
hooks.none: There are no CodeTAC hooks in {file}.
hooks.willRestore: CodeTAC will put {file} back as it was before the install.
hooks.willRemoveFile: CodeTAC will remove {file} (it did not exist before the install).
hooks.willTakeOut: {file} changed since the install: CodeTAC will take out only its own hooks.
hooks.removed: ✓ CodeTAC hooks removed. The prompts already recorded stay in CodeTAC's data folder.
hooks.statusNone: The CodeTAC hooks are not installed here. To install them: codetac hooks install
hooks.statusOn: The CodeTAC hooks are installed in {file}.
hooks.statusOld: The CodeTAC hooks in {file} point to another CodeTAC or folder: run codetac hooks install again.

warmed.one: The project's {count} file is archived once now, so the first prompt is not slowed down.
warmed.other: The project's {count} files are archived once now, so the first prompt is not slowed down.

risk.routeNoAuth: New route {route} possibly without a session check: none of the known ones is in its handler or in the middleware of its file.

report.title: What changed
report.unreadable: The panel did not answer. Is it still running?
report.noProjects: No prompt has been recorded yet. In a project folder, run codetac hooks install; the next prompts given to Claude Code there show up here.
report.noPrompts: No prompt recorded for this project yet.
report.runningNote: Still running: this compares the project before the prompt with the folder as it is now, and updates by itself.
report.interruptedNote: It was interrupted (no end was received): compared up to the next prompt, or to the end of the session.
report.overlapNote: Another prompt was working on the project at the same time: some of these changes may be from it.
report.nothing: Nothing changed in the files of the project.
report.showIt: Show it on the map and in the code
report.mapNote: The plan of the project: added in green, changed in orange, removed with a dashed border. Click a sentence to light what it is about; click a box to see the sentences about it.

codeTitle.one: Code: {count} block of lines ({other} not explained by a sentence)
codeTitle.other: Code: {count} blocks of lines ({other} not explained by a sentence)

report.noteNames: Only the variable names are kept, never the values.
report.noteValues: Only values changed; they are not kept.
report.noteMasked: Keys written in this file are shown masked.
report.outsideTitle: Changes the prompt did not ask for, by the rules, from the request below
report.requestIntro: What did the prompt ask for? The AI can read the prompt and write it as a list of changes; then the rules compare that list with what really changed, and show what was done outside the request. Or write the list yourself.
report.requestRunning: The prompt is still running: the request can be read when it ends.
report.previewTitle: This is exactly what will be sent to {model} ({where}):
report.aiInterpretation: AI interpretation ({model}): check it, and edit it if it is wrong
report.asked: You asked, and it was done
report.askedNone: Nothing of the request shows in the structure.
report.byRules: Compared by rules with the changes in the structure (files, blocks, services), not by the AI. A change inside a file that was asked for counts as asked.
report.editHint: What the prompt asked for, one item per line. Files by their path; blocks as «interface -> logic»; services by their name.
report.editDepends: Blocks that start depending on another
report.editNote: What the prompt asks, in one sentence
report.behaviorRunning: The prompt is still running: run the app's actions again when it ends to compare.
report.behaviorNone: No action of the app was recorded before and after this prompt. To compare what an action does, run it in the app (the same click on the same page) before a prompt and again after it.
report.behaviorNoPair: None of the actions run after the prompt was also run before it (see below).
report.observedTitle: Changes seen when the app ran: the same action before and after the prompt
report.showPath: Show its path on the map
report.sameBehavior: It does the same as before: same requests, functions, outside calls and errors.
report.onlyAfter: Run only after the prompt, so there is no point of comparison: {list}.
report.onlyBefore: Not run again since the prompt (run them in the app to compare): {list}.

behavior.dbStructure: changes the structure of the database ({operation} {tables})

newFunctions.one: «{action}» now runs a function it did not run before: {list}.
newFunctions.other: «{action}» now runs {count} functions it did not run before: {list}.
